content_of_post_to_comment:
Look at how a normal week actually gets built. everyone else's preferences get factored in first. their schedule, their mood, what they'd enjoy, what would be easiest for them. and then whatever's left, whatever fits in the gaps, gets offered to you as your version of a say in things.

you don't even notice it happening most of the time because it's not one big decision. it's dozens of small automatic ones. picking the restaurant nobody else wanted to argue about instead of the one you actually wanted. going along with the later time even though it wrecks your morning. saying it's fine when it's not quite fine, because saying otherwise felt like it would cost more than it was worth in that moment.

each one of these costs almost nothing by itself. that's exactly why it never gets addressed. there's no single moment dramatic enough to point to and say that's the problem. it's just years of defaulting to whatever's easiest for everyone else and calling the leftover option your preference.

somewhere in there you stopped being able to tell the difference between actual flexibility and just never asking for anything. flexibility is a strength when it's a choice. it stops being a strength the moment it's the only mode available, the only thing anyone's ever seen you do.

nobody's going to notice this pattern and fix it for you. it's invisible from the outside precisely because it looks like being easygoing, and easygoing gets rewarded socially, so there's no external signal telling anyone this needs to change.

next time something small comes up, the restaurant, the time, the plan, try naming an actual preference before checking how it'll land. not a dramatic one. just a real one.

see what happens when your comfort gets treated as a starting input instead of the thing that only gets considered once everyone else is already accounted for.
comment: I've noticed the same thing can happen with people who are seen as the 'easygoing one' in a group. The tricky part is that others may genuinely think they're respecting you because you rarely object. Sometimes the first step isn't making bigger demands, it's letting people experience your actual preferences often enough that they become part of the normal conversation.
